title: I Took the Sausage-Stuffer Checkout to the Butcher Who Left My Numbered Casings

parts.text: I stepped into bench one at 6:03 a.m. and butcher Hal was already using my numbered casings. The board said: SIXTY MINUTES. CASINGS STAY WITH THE BOOKING. I was thirty-six, kitchen lead, holding a clipboard that listed our grind. Hal shrugged. "Butchers keep the horn." I photographed the board, the booking, and his grind in my horn. Then I asked for the stuffer checkout. At 6:11 the kitchen desk pinged why Hal's grind sat in our horn. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: The kitchen desk can see Hal's grind in bench one during our hour.

social.video_title: He left his grind in my numbered casings — Part 1/2
social.description: Sausage stuffer, a butcher in my horn, a sixty-minute clock he posted. I logged the grind. Would you have asked for the stuffer checkout?

parts.text: Hal called it test links until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the horn still. The casings went back to my numbered brine. Hal ran a slot of their own and told the next butcher atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: BUTCHERS DO NOT KEEP THE HORN. I keep our grind on a labeled card. Hal brown-bags his links. The bench finally looks like a booking, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Stuffer checkout, numbered casings, and a second line on the board. Were test links ever our grind?
